bracket: [Textbook note (not an error): the stem gives the mass of the oxygen atom as 15.994 u, but the printed working's \(\Delta m = 0.137144\ \mathrm{u}\) is what 15.99486 u gives. Carrying the stem's 15.994 u through instead gives \(\Delta m = 0.138\ \mathrm{u}\), B.E. = 128.53 MeV and \(\overline{B} = 8.03\) MeV per nucleon. The printed 7.98 MeV per nucleon is the physically accurate value; a student who works strictly from the rounded mass in the stem will get 8.03 and is not mistaken.]

[Textbook misprint: the first line of the printed solution reads \(t_{1/2} = \dfrac{0.693}{t_{1/2}}\). The quantity being calculated there is the decay constant, so the left-hand side should be \(\lambda\). The value obtained, \(0.0486\ \mathrm{d^{-1}}\), is correct and is used correctly as \(\lambda\) in every later step, so the answer 14.32 % is unaffected.]

[Textbook misprint, two places, neither affecting the answer as corrected here. (i) The stem gives the atomic mass of \(^{2}\mathrm{H}\) as 2.041 u, while the printed working uses 2.0141 u, which is the correct mass of deuterium; working from the stem's 2.041 u would give \(\Delta m = 0.0466\ \mathrm{u}\) and 43.4 MeV. (ii) The printed last line reads \(E = 0.197\ \mathrm{u} \times 931.4 = 18.35\ \mathrm{MeV}\), but \(0.197 \times 931.4 = 183.5\); the mass defect the working itself obtains is 0.0197 u, and 18.35 MeV is the value that follows from it. The working above has been corrected to 0.0197 u.]

[Textbook answer-key error: the printed last line reads \(2.154 \times 10^{-10}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}} \times 5.763 \times 10^{12}\ \text{atoms} = 1241\ \text{particles}\ \mathrm{s^{-1}}\). The line immediately above it correctly obtains \(N = 5.763 \times 10^{18}\) nuclei, so the exponent 12 is a misprint for 18 and the printed answer 1241 is a factor of \(10^{6}\) too small. The correct activity is \(2.154 \times 10^{-10} \times 5.763 \times 10^{18} = 1.241 \times 10^{9}\) particles per second, and the working above has been corrected to that.]

[Textbook misprint: this question prints only THREE alternatives, (a) to (c) — there is no (d) — and two of the three are genuine fusion reactions. Both (a) and (b) appear in this chapter's own list of the fusion reactions of the Sun and stars (section 13.7.5, reactions (i) and (ii)). Only (c) is not a fusion reaction. The question therefore has no single correct answer, and it is presented here as a free-response question with the three printed alternatives in the stem rather than as a multiple-choice question with an invented fourth option.]

[Textbook misprint: alternative (d) is printed as \(_{14}\mathrm{Si}\), with an atomic number but no mass number. It is wrong either way, since balancing the reaction requires \(Z = 15\), but as printed it cannot even be tested against the mass-number balance.]

[Textbook misprint: the parent nuclide is printed as \(^{60}_{27}\mathrm{CO}\), with a capital O. The element of atomic number 27 is cobalt, whose symbol is Co; CO is carbon monoxide. The nuclide meant is \(^{60}_{27}\mathrm{Co}\), which the chapter itself lists in Table 13.4 (b) with a half life of 5.3 years.]

[Textbook misprint: the product iodine nuclide is printed with the numbers after the symbol and with the subscript 54, the same atomic number as the xenon it comes from. Read literally the missing particle would have \(A = 0\) and \(Z = 0\), that is nothing at all. The atomic number of iodine is 53, so the product is \(^{118}_{53}\mathrm{I}\), and the answer below uses that value.]

[Textbook misprint, two places. (i) The fifth nuclide is printed as \(^{28}_{14}\mathrm{S}\): — the element of atomic number 14 is silicon, so the trailing colon is the letter i and the nuclide is \(^{28}_{14}\mathrm{Si}\). (ii) As the five nuclides are printed, no two of them share a mass number, so the list contains NO pair of mirror nuclei and that half of the question cannot be answered. Reading the first entry as \(^{11}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) rather than \(^{10}_{5}\mathrm{B}\) makes it and \(^{11}_{6}\mathrm{C}\) a mirror pair and leaves two clean isotone pairs, which is very probably what was intended.]

[Textbook misprint: the first of the four fusion reactions printed in section 13.7.5 is given as \(^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{1}_{1}\mathrm{H} \longrightarrow {}^{2}_{1}\mathrm{H} + {}^{0}_{-1}\mathrm{e}\), which does not balance in charge — the left-hand side carries \(+2\) and the right-hand side \(1 - 1 = 0\). The emitted particle is a positron, \(^{0}_{1}\mathrm{e}\), which makes both sides \(+2\); the same reaction is printed with the positron in exercise 1 (A) of this chapter. The answer below gives the balanced form.]

[Textbook misprint / answer-key error, two places. (i) The stem reads "How many - particles", with the particle symbol missing before the hyphen; radium-226 is an \(\alpha\)-emitter (section 13.6.1), so these are \(\alpha\)-particles. (ii) The stem gives no half life, and the printed answer \(1.154 \times 10^{17}\) is what \(t_{1/2} = 1600\) y would give — but the only half life this chapter supplies for radium-226 is 1620 y, in Table 13.4 (b), and that gives \(1.14 \times 10^{17}\). The printed answer therefore contradicts the chapter's own table.]
